Pathology-01.question: ১) Which is not a type of cellular adaptation?
Pathology-01.exp:
Cellular adaptations are reversible changes that allow cells to respond to physiological or pathological stress. The major types of cellular adaptation are hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, and metaplasia.

Dysplasia is not considered a true cellular adaptation. It refers to disordered growth and maturation of cells, characterized by variations in cell size, shape, and nuclear appearance. Dysplasia is considered a premalignant change and may progress to carcinoma if the underlying cause persists.

The other options are true types of cellular adaptation:

  • Metaplasia: Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another.

  • Hyperplasia: Increase in the number of cells.

  • Hypertrophy: Increase in the size of cells.

Pathology-01.question: ২) Which enzyme does not take part in destruction of free radicals?
Pathology-01.exp:
Free radicals and reactive oxygen species (ROS) are neutralized by several antioxidant enzymes that protect cells from oxidative injury. The major antioxidant enzymes include:

  • Superoxide dismutase (SOD), which converts superoxide radicals (O₂⁻) into hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂).

  • Catalase, which converts H₂O₂ into water and oxygen.

  • Glutathione peroxidase, which reduces H₂O₂ and lipid peroxides to harmless products using reduced glutathione (GSH).

In contrast, myeloperoxidase (MPO) does not participate in the destruction of free radicals. Instead, it uses H₂O₂ and chloride ions to generate hypochlorous acid (HOCl), a potent oxidant that helps neutrophils kill microorganisms during the respiratory burst.

Pathology-01.question: ৩) The antioxidant found in the body excludes—
Pathology-01.exp:
The body has several endogenous antioxidants that protect cells from damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS). These include both antioxidant enzymes and antioxidant-binding proteins.

  • Serum albumin acts as an antioxidant by scavenging free radicals and binding transition metals.

  • Transferrin binds iron, preventing it from participating in free radical formation through the Fenton reaction.

  • Ceruloplasmin binds and oxidizes copper, reducing its ability to generate reactive oxygen species.

Cobalamin (vitamin B₁₂) is an essential vitamin involved in DNA synthesis and neurological function, but it is not classified as one of the body's endogenous antioxidant defense mechanisms in standard pathology.

Pathology-01.question: ৪) Which is not a hallmark of reversible cell injury?
Pathology-01.exp:
The hallmark of reversible cell injury is cellular swelling (hydropic change), which results from ATP depletion due to reduced oxidative phosphorylation. ATP depletion impairs the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, causing sodium and water to move into the cell, leading to water influx and cell swelling.

Water efflux (movement of water out of the cell) does not occur in reversible cell injury. Instead, the cell gains water and becomes swollen.

The other options are features of reversible cell injury:

  • ATP depletion is an early biochemical event.

  • Reduced oxidative phosphorylation decreases ATP production.

  • Cellular swelling is the earliest and most characteristic morphological change.

Pathology-01.question: ৫) Caseation necrosis commonly occurs in---
Pathology-01.exp:
Caseation necrosis is a distinctive form of necrosis characterized by soft, friable, cheese-like white-yellow necrotic material. Microscopically, it shows amorphous granular debris with complete loss of cellular architecture and is typically surrounded by granulomatous inflammation.

Tuberculosis is the classic disease associated with caseating granulomas and caseation necrosis due to the host's cell-mediated immune response against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sarcoidosis typically produces non-caseating granulomas.

  • Actinomycosis causes suppurative (abscess-forming) inflammation with sulfur granules rather than caseation.

  • Gas gangrene is characterized by coagulative necrosis with myonecrosis caused by Clostridium species.

Difficulty: Easy

Pathology-01.question: ৬) Which is not a type of nuclear change in irreversible cell injury?
Pathology-01.exp:
In irreversible cell injury, the nucleus undergoes characteristic degenerative changes:

  • Pyknosis: Nuclear shrinkage with increased basophilia due to chromatin condensation.

  • Karyorrhexis: Fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus.

  • Karyolysis: Dissolution and fading of the nucleus due to enzymatic degradation of DNA.

Karyokinesis is not a degenerative nuclear change. It is the process of nuclear division during mitosis in normal cell proliferation.

Pathology-01.question: ৭) Chalky white area found in which type of necrosis?
Pathology-01.exp:
Fat necrosis is characterized by chalky white deposits due to fat saponification. In this process, fatty acids released from damaged adipose tissue combine with calcium to form insoluble calcium soaps, producing the characteristic chalky white appearance.

This type of necrosis is classically seen in acute pancreatitis, where pancreatic lipases digest peripancreatic fat, and in traumatic fat necrosis, especially of the breast.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fibrinoid necrosis shows bright eosinophilic, fibrin-like deposits in blood vessel walls.

  • Gangrenous necrosis refers to ischemic necrosis of a limb or bowel and appears dry or wet rather than chalky white.

  • Caseous necrosis has a soft, cheese-like appearance, classically seen in tuberculosis.

Pathology-01.question: ৮) What is the most fertile soil for malignant transformation?
Pathology-01.exp:
Metaplastic epithelium is considered the most fertile soil for malignant transformation because persistent irritation or chronic inflammation can cause epithelial metaplasia, which may progress to dysplasia and eventually carcinoma if the underlying stimulus continues.

Common examples include:

  • Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium in smokers, which may progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Barrett esophagus (intestinal metaplasia), which increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

The other options are incorrect because muscle, nerve fibers, and bone do not undergo clinically significant metaplastic changes that serve as common precursors to malignancy.

Pathology-01.question: ৯) Which enzyme is responsible for apoptosis?
Pathology-01.exp:
Caspases are the key enzymes responsible for apoptosis (programmed cell death). They are synthesized as inactive procaspases and become activated through the intrinsic (mitochondrial) or extrinsic (death receptor) pathway. Once activated, initiator caspases activate executioner caspases, which degrade structural proteins, activate endonucleases, and fragment DNA, leading to controlled cell death without provoking inflammation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Catalase is an antioxidant enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

  • Myeloperoxidase generates hypochlorous acid (HOCl) in neutrophils to kill microorganisms.

  • Hydroxylase enzymes catalyze hydroxylation reactions and are not involved in apoptosis.

Pathology-01.question: ১০) The uterus decreases in size after parturition by which process?
Pathology-01.exp:
After parturition, the uterus gradually returns to its pre-pregnancy size through physiological atrophy (involution). During pregnancy, the uterus enlarges mainly due to hypertrophy of smooth muscle cells, with some contribution from hyperplasia. After delivery, the hormonal stimulus declines, leading to decreased protein synthesis and proteolysis of excess cellular components. As a result, the enlarged smooth muscle cells decrease in size, causing uterine involution.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypertrophy increases cell size and occurs during pregnancy, not after delivery.

  • Metaplasia is the replacement of one mature cell type by another.

  • Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells and contributes to uterine enlargement during pregnancy.

Pathology-01.question: ১১) Which one is the predominant inflammatory cell in viral infection?
Pathology-01.exp:
In viral infections, the predominant inflammatory cells are lymphocytes, particularly T lymphocytes, which play a central role in the immune response by recognizing and destroying virus-infected cells. Therefore, viral infections typically produce a lymphocytic infiltrate.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutrophils predominate in acute bacterial infections.

  • Macrophages are the principal cells in chronic inflammation and granulomatous diseases.

  • Eosinophils are characteristically increased in parasitic infections and allergic disorders.

Pathology-01.question: ১২) Which is not one of the step of phagocytosis?
Pathology-01.exp:
Phagocytosis is the process by which phagocytic cells, such as neutrophils and macrophages, ingest and destroy microorganisms or dead cells. The main steps of phagocytosis are:

  • Recognition and attachment of the target (often enhanced by opsonization).

  • Engulfment, forming a phagosome.

  • Killing and degradation after fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes.

Chemotaxis is the directed movement of leukocytes toward the site of infection or tissue injury in response to chemical attractants. It occurs before phagocytosis and is part of leukocyte recruitment, not one of the actual steps of phagocytosis.

Pathology-01.question: ১৩) Common cold is an example of which type of inflammation?
Pathology-01.exp:
Common cold is a classic example of catarrhal inflammation, which affects mucous membranes. It is characterized by excessive mucus secretion due to inflammation of the respiratory mucosa, commonly caused by viral infections such as rhinovirus.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Necrotizing inflammation is characterized by tissue destruction and necrosis.

  • Fibrinous inflammation involves the deposition of fibrin-rich exudate, typically seen in conditions such as fibrinous pericarditis.

  • Serous inflammation produces a thin, watery, protein-poor fluid, as seen in skin blisters following burns or viral infections.

Pathology-01.question: ১৪) Which is not a criteria of dry gangrene?
Pathology-01.exp:
Dry gangrene results from loss of arterial blood supply, usually affecting the limbs. It develops slowly, allowing the tissue to become dry, shrunken, and black due to coagulative necrosis. Since there is little or no bacterial infection, venous drainage is usually preserved until late in the process.

A characteristic feature of dry gangrene is the presence of a well-defined line of demarcation, which clearly separates the viable tissue from the dead tissue.

Therefore, "line of demarcation absent" is not a feature of dry gangrene. It is more typical of wet gangrene, where the infection spreads rapidly and the boundary between healthy and necrotic tissue is poorly defined.

Pathology-01.question: ১৫) Aschoff giant cell is found in---?
Pathology-01.exp:
Aschoff giant cells are characteristic of Aschoff bodies, the pathognomonic lesion of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. These multinucleated giant cells are formed by activated macrophages and are found within the myocardium along with Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells, lymphocytes, and fibrinoid necrosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Tuberculosis is characterized by Langhans giant cells within caseating granulomas.

  • Lymphoma does not contain Aschoff giant cells; Reed–Sternberg cells are characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

  • Syphilis produces gummatous inflammation and plasma cell-rich infiltrates rather than Aschoff bodies.

Pathology-01.question: ১৬) Oedema is clinically evident when there is an excess of fluid by---?
Pathology-01.exp:
Edema becomes clinically evident only after a substantial amount of fluid has accumulated in the interstitial tissues. In general, it is detectable when there is an increase of approximately 2.5–3 liters of interstitial fluid, which corresponds to about 15% excess fluid.

This is why mild fluid retention may not produce visible swelling, whereas more significant accumulation results in pitting edema or generalized swelling.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 10% is usually insufficient for clinically apparent edema.

  • 20% and 50% represent much greater fluid accumulation than is required for edema to become clinically evident.

Pathology-01.question: ১৭) Which is not a feature of exudate?
Pathology-01.exp:
Exudate is an inflammatory fluid formed due to increased vascular permeability. It is characterized by a high protein content, the presence of fibrinogen, and numerous inflammatory cells. Because of its high protein concentration, the specific gravity is typically greater than 1.020.

A specific gravity below 1.012 is a feature of transudate, which results from non-inflammatory conditions such as increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased plasma oncotic pressure.

Therefore, specific gravity below 1.012 is not a feature of exudate.

Pathology-01.question: ১৮) Migration of leukocyte to the site of injury is termed as--?
Pathology-01.exp:
Chemotaxis is the directed migration of leukocytes toward the site of tissue injury or infection in response to chemical attractants such as C5a, IL-8, LTB₄, and bacterial products. It is an essential step in the inflammatory response, guiding leukocytes to the area where they are needed.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Diapedesis is the passage of leukocytes through the intact vascular endothelium into the extravascular tissue.

  • Opsonization is the coating of microorganisms with opsonins (e.g., IgG, C3b) to facilitate phagocytosis.

  • Phagocytosis is the ingestion and destruction of microorganisms or cellular debris by phagocytic cells.

Pathology-01.question: ১৯) Which is not permanent cell on the basis of regenerative capacity?
Pathology-01.exp:
Based on their regenerative capacity, cells are classified as labile, stable, and permanent.

Permanent cells have permanently left the cell cycle and have little or no capacity to regenerate after injury. They include:

  • Nerve cells (neurons)

  • Cardiac muscle cells

  • Skeletal muscle cells (very limited regeneration through satellite cells, but mature muscle fibers are considered permanent)

In contrast, smooth muscle cells are stable cells, not permanent cells. They retain the ability to proliferate in response to injury or increased functional demand, such as during pregnancy or after vascular injury.

Pathology-01.question: ২০) Which one is the local factor that influence wound healing?
Pathology-01.exp:
Factors affecting wound healing are broadly classified into local and systemic factors.

Infection is the most important local factor delaying wound healing. It prolongs inflammation, causes tissue destruction, increases wound exudate, and interferes with collagen synthesis and wound contraction.

The other options are systemic factors:

  • Protein deficiency impairs collagen synthesis and tissue repair.

  • Diabetes mellitus delays healing by causing poor blood supply, impaired leukocyte function, and increased susceptibility to infection.

  • Steroids suppress inflammation and inhibit fibroblast proliferation and collagen formation.

Pathology-01.question: ২১) Which doesn't happen by excessive formation of repair tissue?
Pathology-01.exp:
Excessive formation of repair tissue results from excessive collagen deposition or an exaggerated healing response. It can lead to:

  • Keloid – excessive scar tissue extending beyond the original wound margins.

  • Hypertrophic scar – excessive collagen confined to the original wound margins.

  • Desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis) – a fibroblastic proliferation that may arise in areas of previous trauma or surgical scars.

In contrast, wound dehiscence is caused by inadequate wound healing, where the wound ruptures due to insufficient collagen formation or reduced wound strength. It is associated with factors such as infection, poor nutrition, diabetes, corticosteroid therapy, or increased wound tension, rather than excessive repair tissue.

Pathology-01.question: ২২) Which of the following is the example of non pitting oedema?
Pathology-01.exp:
Lymphedema is a classic example of non-pitting edema. It results from obstruction or impaired drainage of lymphatic vessels, leading to the accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid. Over time, chronic inflammation and fibrosis make the affected tissue firm, so pressure does not leave a persistent indentation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatic edema is usually pitting edema, caused by hypoalbuminemia and portal hypertension.

  • Cardiac edema is typically pitting edema, resulting from increased venous hydrostatic pressure.

  • Renal edema is also pitting edema, commonly due to sodium and water retention or hypoalbuminemia in nephrotic syndrome.

Pathology-01.question: ২৩) Which is not a common site for passive congestion?
Pathology-01.exp:
Passive congestion is the accumulation of blood in an organ due to impaired venous outflow. It commonly affects organs with rich venous drainage, especially:

  • Lungs – seen in left-sided heart failure, causing pulmonary congestion.

  • Liver – seen in right-sided heart failure, producing the characteristic nutmeg liver.

  • Spleen – may become congested in conditions such as portal hypertension or chronic venous congestion.

The lymph node is not a common site of passive congestion because it is primarily part of the lymphatic system rather than the venous circulation.

Pathology-01.question: ২৪) Virchow’s triad does not include---?
Pathology-01.exp:
Virchow's triad describes the three major factors that predispose to thrombosis:

  • Endothelial injury

  • Alteration of normal blood flow (stasis or turbulence)

  • Hypercoagulability of blood

These factors promote thrombus formation by damaging the vascular endothelium, disrupting normal blood flow, or increasing the tendency of blood to clot.

Hypocoagulability refers to a reduced tendency to form clots, leading to bleeding rather than thrombosis. Therefore, it is not a component of Virchow's triad.

Pathology-01.question: ২৫) Red infarct does not occur in---?
Pathology-01.exp:
Red (hemorrhagic) infarcts occur in tissues with dual blood supply, loose tissue architecture, venous occlusion, or after reperfusion of an ischemic area. Common examples include:

  • Lung – because of its dual blood supply from the pulmonary and bronchial arteries.

  • Small intestine – due to its rich collateral circulation and loose tissue.

  • Ovary – especially following venous outflow obstruction such as torsion.

In contrast, the heart has an end-arterial circulation with limited collateral blood supply. Occlusion of a coronary artery typically produces a white (anemic) infarct, making hemorrhagic infarction uncommon.

Pathology-01.question: ২৬) Hemorrhagic shock occurs with acute loss of blood about---of total blood?
Pathology-01.exp:
Hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock develops when there is a rapid loss of a significant volume of blood, resulting in inadequate tissue perfusion. In general, acute loss of about 20–25% of the total blood volume is sufficient to produce hemorrhagic shock if not promptly corrected. Among the given options, 25% is the best answer.

Lesser blood loss (around 15%) is usually compensated by sympathetic mechanisms. With increasing blood loss (around 30–40% or more), shock becomes severe, with marked hypotension, tissue hypoperfusion, and risk of irreversible organ damage.

Pathology-01.question: ২৭) How many stages of shock are there?
Pathology-01.exp:
Shock is classically divided into three stages based on the progression of tissue hypoperfusion and the reversibility of organ damage:

  • Non-progressive (compensated) stage: Compensatory mechanisms such as tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system maintain tissue perfusion.

  • Progressive (decompensated) stage: Compensatory mechanisms fail, leading to worsening tissue hypoperfusion, metabolic acidosis, and organ dysfunction.

  • Irreversible (refractory) stage: Severe cellular and organ injury occurs, and recovery is unlikely even if the underlying cause is corrected.

Although some trauma classifications describe four classes of hemorrhagic shock based on the amount of blood loss, the pathological stages of shock are three.

Pathology-01.question: ২৮) Generalized oedema is termed as –?
Pathology-01.exp:
Anasarca refers to severe generalized edema, characterized by widespread accumulation of fluid in the subcutaneous tissues and interstitial spaces throughout the body. It is commonly seen in conditions such as heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, and severe hypoproteinemia.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ascites is the accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

  • Hydrothorax is the accumulation of non-inflammatory (transudative) fluid in the pleural cavity.

  • Pleural effusion is a general term for fluid in the pleural cavity, which may be either transudative or exudative.

Pathology-01.question: ২৯) Trisomy 18 is known as --?
Pathology-01.exp:
Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy 18, in which there is an extra copy of chromosome 18. It is characterized by severe developmental delay, prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart defects. Most affected infants have a poor prognosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21.

  • Patau syndrome is caused by trisomy 13.

  • Turner syndrome is caused by monosomy X (45,X).

Pathology-01.question: ৩০) Which is not an example of autosomal dominant disorder?
Pathology-01.exp:
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired copper excretion and excessive copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and cornea.

The other options are all autosomal dominant disorders:

  • Marfan syndrome – mutation in the FBN1 gene.

  • Tuberous sclerosis – mutation in the TSC1 or TSC2 gene.

  • Achondroplasia – mutation in the FGFR3 gene.

Therefore, Wilson disease is the only option that is not inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

Pathology-01.question: ৩১) Which is x-linked dominant disorder?
Pathology-01.exp:
Vitamin D–resistant rickets (also known as X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets) is the most common X-linked dominant disorder. It is caused by mutations in the PHEX gene, leading to renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, and defective bone mineralization.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders.

  • Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive disorder.

  • Sickle cell disease is also an autosomal recessive disorder.

Pathology-01.question: ৩২) Malignant tumor of mesenchymal tissue is called--?
Pathology-01.exp:
A sarcoma is a malignant tumor of mesenchymal (connective) tissue. It arises from tissues such as bone, cartilage, muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, and blood vessels. Examples include osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, liposarcoma, and leiomyosarcoma.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Carcinoma is a malignant tumor arising from epithelial tissue.

  • Cancer is a general term for all malignant neoplasms, including both carcinomas and sarcomas.

  • Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes, which are neural crest-derived cells.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৩) Karyotype of turner’s syndrome is--?
Pathology-01.exp:
Turner syndrome is caused by complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome, with the classic karyotype being 45,XO. Affected individuals are phenotypic females and commonly present with short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, streak ovaries, and primary amenorrhea. They are also at increased risk of coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 47,XXY = Klinefelter syndrome.

  • 47,XX,+21 = Down syndrome (Trisomy 21).

  • 47,XX,+18 = Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18).

Pathology-01.question: ৩৪) Rhabdomyoma is a benign tumor of which tissue?
Pathology-01.exp:
A rhabdomyoma is a benign tumor of striated (skeletal) muscle. The prefix "rhabdo-" refers to striated skeletal muscle, while "-myoma" denotes a benign tumor. Its malignant counterpart is rhabdomyosarcoma.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Smooth muscle gives rise to leiomyoma (benign) and leiomyosarcoma (malignant).

  • Cardiac muscle can rarely develop cardiac rhabdomyoma, but in standard tumor nomenclature, rhabdomyoma refers to a benign tumor of skeletal (striated) muscle.

  • Fat cells give rise to lipoma (benign) and liposarcoma (malignant).

Pathology-01.question: ৩৫) Philadelphia chromosome is found in--?
Pathology-01.exp:
The Philadelphia chromosome is the characteristic cytogenetic abnormality of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It results from a reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11), which creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene. This fusion gene encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, leading to uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells.

Although the Philadelphia chromosome may also be present in a subset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), especially in adults, it is classically and most strongly associated with CML. Therefore, the single best answer is CML.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AML is associated with other chromosomal abnormalities, such as t(15;17) in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

  • ALL may rarely be Philadelphia chromosome-positive but it is not the classic association.

  • CLL has no characteristic Philadelphia chromosome.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৬) Which is not criteria of benign tumor?
Pathology-01.exp:
Benign tumors are characterized by well-differentiated cells, slow growth, and absence of metastasis. They closely resemble the tissue of origin and usually have uniform cell and nuclear morphology.

Pleomorphism, which refers to marked variation in the size and shape of cells and nuclei, is a feature of anaplasia and is characteristic of malignant tumors, not benign tumors.

The other options are typical features of benign tumors:

  • Well differentiated

  • Slow rate of growth

  • No metastasis

Pathology-01.question: ৩৭) All of the followings are locally malignant tumor except--?
Pathology-01.exp:
A locally malignant tumor is one that is highly invasive at its site of origin but has little or no tendency to metastasize.

Examples include:

  • Basal cell carcinoma – locally aggressive with metastasis being extremely rare.

  • Glioma – extensively infiltrates the surrounding brain tissue but rarely metastasizes outside the central nervous system.

In contrast, squamous cell carcinoma is a true malignant tumor that has the potential for both local invasion and metastasis, particularly through the lymphatics. Therefore, it is not classified as a locally malignant tumor.

Although carcinoid tumors are generally low-grade malignant neoplasms, they also possess metastatic potential and are not classically categorized as "locally malignant." However, among the given options, squamous cell carcinoma is the best single answer because it is a typical metastatic carcinoma rather than a locally malignant lesion.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৮) Which is not oncogenic virus??
Pathology-01.exp:
Oncogenic viruses are viruses that contribute directly to the development of cancer by inducing genetic or cellular changes.

The following are well-established oncogenic viruses:

  • HPV (Human papillomavirus) – associated with cervical carcinoma, anogenital cancers, and oropharyngeal cancers.

  • EBV (Epstein–Barr virus) – associated with Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and some gastric cancers.

  • HBV (Hepatitis B virus) – associated with hepatocellular carcinoma through chronic inflammation and viral effects.

HIV is not directly oncogenic. It increases the risk of malignancies such as Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and cervical cancer by causing immunosuppression, which impairs immune surveillance and allows oncogenic viruses (e.g., HHV-8, EBV, and HPV) to promote tumor development.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৯) Which one is tumor marker for breast cancer?
Pathology-01.exp:
CA 15-3 is the tumor marker most commonly associated with breast cancer. It is primarily used to monitor response to treatment, detect recurrence, and assess disease progression in patients with known breast cancer. It is not suitable for screening or establishing the initial diagnosis because its sensitivity and specificity are limited.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CA-125 is mainly associated with epithelial ovarian cancer.

  • CA 19-9 is primarily used in pancreatic cancer and some gastrointestinal malignancies.

  • CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is a nonspecific tumor marker, commonly used in colorectal cancer, although it may also be elevated in breast and other cancers.

Pathology-01.question: ৪০) Paget’s disease is precancerous lesion for--?
Pathology-01.exp:
Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is a chronic disorder characterized by excessive and disorganized bone remodeling. Although most patients remain benign, a small proportion develop osteosarcoma or other bone sarcomas. Therefore, Paget disease of bone is considered a premalignant (precancerous) condition for bone.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Stomach has premalignant conditions such as chronic atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia.

  • Colon has premalignant lesions such as adenomatous polyps.

  • Liver is predisposed to hepatocellular carcinoma by chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, not Paget disease.

Pathology-01.question: ৪১) Prenatal diagnosis can’t be from ---?
Pathology-01.exp:
Prenatal diagnostic tests are traditionally performed using fetal-derived samples, such as:

  • Amniotic fluid (amniocentesis)

  • Chorionic villi (chorionic villus sampling)

  • Fetal cord blood (cordocentesis)

These methods allow direct analysis of fetal cells or fetal blood for chromosomal, genetic, and some hematological disorders.

Although maternal peripheral blood can now be used for non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) by analyzing cell-free fetal DNA, it is considered a screening test, not a definitive diagnostic test. Any abnormal NIPT result requires confirmation with an invasive diagnostic procedure such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling.

Pathology-01.question: ৪২) Which is not a feature of klinefelter’s syndrome?
Pathology-01.exp:
Klinefelter syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra X chromosome, with the classic karyotype being 47,XXY. It is characterized by primary hypogonadism, small testes, male infertility, tall stature with long limbs, and often gynecomastia.

The other options are true features of Klinefelter syndrome:

  • Hypogonadism is a characteristic finding.

  • Male infertility results from impaired spermatogenesis.

  • Tall stature is a common physical feature.

47,XYY is a different chromosomal disorder known as XYY syndrome (Jacob syndrome) and is not the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৩) Anti tumor immune mechanism exclude--?
Pathology-01.exp:
The major anti-tumor immune effector mechanisms include:

  • Natural killer (NK) cells, which destroy tumor cells without prior sensitization.

  • Activated macrophages, which kill tumor cells through cytokines and reactive oxygen/nitrogen intermediates.

  • Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), in which NK cells and other effector cells kill antibody-coated tumor cells.

Helper T lymphocytes (CD4⁺ T cells) do not directly kill tumor cells. Their primary role is to coordinate the immune response by secreting cytokines that activate cytotoxic T lymphocytes, macrophages, and NK cells. Therefore, they are not considered a direct anti-tumor effector mechanism.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৪) Hyperplasia does not occur in ---?
Pathology-01.exp:
Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells and occurs only in tissues capable of cell division.

It occurs in:

  • Pregnant uterus – due to estrogen-induced hyperplasia (along with hypertrophy) of uterine smooth muscle.

  • Wound healing – through proliferation of fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells.

  • BEP is likely a typographical error for BPH (Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia), a classic example of pathological hyperplasia.

In cardiomyopathy, cardiac muscle cells are permanent cells and cannot undergo hyperplasia. They respond to increased workload by hypertrophy (increase in cell size) rather than an increase in cell number.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৫) In grade-I cancer ---cell differentiation occurs?
Pathology-01.exp:
Tumor grading is based on the degree of differentiation of tumor cells.

Grade I (well-differentiated) cancers have more than 75% cell differentiation, meaning that most tumor cells closely resemble the normal cells from which they arise. These tumors generally grow more slowly and have a better prognosis than higher-grade tumors.

A commonly used grading system is:

  • Grade I: >75% differentiation (well differentiated)

  • Grade II: 50–75% differentiation (moderately differentiated)

  • Grade III: 25–50% differentiation (poorly differentiated)

  • Grade IV: <25% differentiation (undifferentiated/anaplastic)

Pathology-01.question: ৪৬) Which is not a type phagocytic cell?
Pathology-01.exp:
Phagocytic cells are specialized cells that engulf and destroy microorganisms, dead cells, and cellular debris.

Major phagocytic cells include:

  • Neutrophils – the first responders in acute inflammation and highly efficient phagocytes.

  • Macrophages – professional phagocytes derived from monocytes.

  • Kupffer cells – specialized macrophages located in the liver that remove microorganisms and aged red blood cells from the blood.

Lymphocytes (B cells, T cells, and NK cells) are responsible for adaptive and innate immune responses, but they are not phagocytic cells.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৭) Which is not a tumor suppressive gene?
Pathology-01.exp:
The question appears to contain a typing error. The intended option is most likely K-ras, which is a well-known proto-oncogene, not a tumor suppressor gene.

Tumor suppressor genes normally inhibit cell proliferation, repair DNA damage, or promote apoptosis. Loss or inactivation of these genes contributes to tumor development. Examples include:

  • p53 – the "guardian of the genome"

  • RB (Retinoblastoma gene) – regulates the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint

  • BRCA1 – involved in DNA repair

In contrast, K-ras is a proto-oncogene. When activated by mutation, it becomes an oncogene, promoting uncontrolled cell growth and proliferation.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৮) The following conditions are considered precancerous except--?
Pathology-01.exp:
A precancerous (premalignant) lesion is a morphologically altered tissue that has an increased risk of progressing to cancer.

The following are recognized precancerous lesions:

  • Solar (actinic) keratosis – may progress to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Leukoplakia – especially in the oral cavity, has the potential to develop into squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Erythroplakia – has a higher risk of malignant transformation than leukoplakia and often shows severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by epidermal hyperproliferation. It is not considered a precancerous lesion. Although the risk of skin cancer may increase in some patients due to long-term immunosuppressive therapy or PUVA treatment, psoriasis itself is not a premalignant condition.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৯) Which Tumor arise from more than one germ layer?
Pathology-01.exp:
A teratoma is a tumor derived from totipotent germ cells and contains tissues originating from more than one germ layer—ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. It may be benign (mature teratoma) or malignant (immature teratoma), depending on the degree of differentiation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor arising from a single germ layer (ectoderm or endoderm-derived epithelium).

  • Carcinoma is a malignant tumor of epithelial origin.

  • Sarcoma is a malignant tumor of mesenchymal tissue, which is derived from the mesoderm.

Pathology-01.question: ৫০) Which is not an example of dormant cancer?
Pathology-01.exp:
Dormant cancers are tumors that may remain clinically silent for prolonged periods before recurring or producing metastases. This phenomenon is due to tumor dormancy, where malignant cells persist in a non-proliferative or slowly proliferative state.

Examples include:

  • Breast carcinoma – may recur many years after initial treatment.

  • Malignant melanoma – well known for late recurrence after a prolonged disease-free interval.

  • Neuroblastoma – some cases may remain quiescent or even undergo spontaneous regression, particularly in infants.

In contrast, choriocarcinoma is a highly aggressive and rapidly growing malignant trophoblastic tumor. It metastasizes early but is highly sensitive to chemotherapy. It is not considered a classic example of a dormant cancer.
